title: The Girl Who Was There
author: Barbara W. Tuchman
wiifm: Gibbon's clock ran for three centuries. This one runs for thirty days. Tuchman's subject is how competent, sane, professional men walked a whole civilisation into a catastrophe none of them wanted, not through wickedness or stupidity, but through plans that could not be stopped once started. It is also the only book on this list that can be argued to have changed history, because a president read it in 1962 and behaved differently for having done so. And the woman who wrote it was physically present, aged two, at the moment the war began.

b: A small Italian steamer came into Constantinople on 10 August 1914, carrying among its passengers the American ambassador's daughter, her husband, and three of the ambassador's grandchildren. The youngest was two and a half years old. Her name was Barbara Wertheim.

On the way, that ship had been in the middle of something. The German battlecruiser Goeben and the light cruiser Breslau were running for the Dardanelles with the Royal Navy in pursuit, and the little steamer had found itself in the middle of a naval chase that would end with the two German ships being handed to the Ottoman Empire, one of the hinges on which Turkey entered the war on Germany's side, which in turn shaped the Middle East for the next century.

Forty-eight years later she published a book about the first month of that war, and she put the scene of that ship's arrival in it. She did not mention that she had been aboard. Readers only learned it later, when she identified herself as a passenger in a collection of essays.

Start here, because it tells you what kind of historian she was. She had an unrepeatable personal claim on the material and she kept it out of the book, because the book was not about her. That discipline, the refusal to put herself at the centre of a story she happened to be in, is the same discipline that makes her narrative of August 1914 trustworthy even where her causal arguments are not.
ch.cap: A small steamer reaches Constantinople as warships run past

b: Barbara Wertheim was born in New York in January 1912 into money and proximity to power. Her father was a banker who owned The Nation. Her grandfather, Henry Morgenthau, was Woodrow Wilson's ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, which is why she was on that ship. Her uncle became Roosevelt's Treasury Secretary.

She took a degree in history and literature at Radcliffe in 1933 and then never acquired a graduate qualification of any kind. She was, in the professional sense, an amateur for her entire career, and she said plainly that she thought academic writing conventions would have ruined her.

What she did instead was work. Research at the Institute of Pacific Relations, a year in Tokyo, travel in China, reporting on the Spanish Civil War for her father's magazine, then the Office of War Information during the Second World War. She married a physician in 1940, raised three daughters, and only turned to history properly in her forties, producing a book roughly every four years thereafter.

The Guns of August appeared in 1962, when she was fifty. It won the Pulitzer Prize for General Non-fiction, it was ineligible for the History prize, which Joseph Pulitzer's will restricts to American history. She won a second Pulitzer in 1972. She died in 1989.

After The Guns of August she kept moving backwards and forwards through the same troubled century and beyond it: The Proud Tower, on the world before the war; a life of General Stilwell in China, which won her second Pulitzer; A Distant Mirror, on the calamitous fourteenth century; and The March of Folly, on governments pursuing policies against their own interests. Her method never changed. She visited the ground, read the letters and diaries, and treated the narrative itself as the argument.

The lesson is not that credentials are worthless. It is that she had no professional incentive to write for other historians, and so she wrote for readers, and the result has outlived almost all of the scholarship produced alongside it.
ch.cap: Barbara, no degree in history, types for ordinary readers

ch.h: Nine kings in black and gold
b: The book opens on a May morning in 1910, with nine reigning kings riding through London behind the coffin of Edward VII, and a black-clad crowd gasping at the sight of them. It is one of the great openings in English non-fiction, and it is doing precise work.

Look at who those men were. Cousins, most of them. Professional, educated, in several cases personally decent, none of them mad. The German Kaiser, the British King and the Russian Tsar were all grandsons or grandsons-in-law of Victoria. Within a dozen years of that procession, four empires represented in it, the German, the Russian, the Austro-Hungarian and the Ottoman, had ceased to exist, and something like twenty million people were dead.

Tuchman puts the funeral first so that you cannot reach for the easy explanation. There is no villain in the opening chapter and no idiot. What follows is not a story about bad men; it is a story about a design.

This is the single most useful habit the book can give you, and it transfers directly. When something fails badly, the instinct is to find the person responsible. Tuchman's instinct is to look at the mechanism that made competent people behave that way, which is the same move Perrow makes with control rooms and Meadows makes with systems.
ch.cap: Nine kings ride behind Edward VII's coffin, May 1910

ch.h: The plan that owned its makers
b: Germany's problem was geography: France to the west, Russia to the east, no realistic prospect of fighting both at once. Count Alfred von Schlieffen, chief of the general staff until 1906, produced the answer that carries his name. Put almost everything in the west, swing an enormous right wing through Belgium, envelop Paris, destroy the French army in six weeks, then move the whole force east by rail before Russia can fully mobilise.
It was an engineering solution to a political problem, and it had one fatal property: it only worked at full speed, in one direction, all at once. There was no version of it you could do partially.

Schlieffen's successor was Helmuth von Moltke the Younger, nephew of the Moltke who had beaten France in 1870 and burdened for life by the comparison. He kept the plan and hedged it, strengthening the left wing in Alsace-Lorraine, because the thought of German soil being occupied even briefly was politically unbearable, thereby weakening the wing on which everything depended.

Schlieffen died in January 1913, the year before his plan was tested. The story goes that his last words were a plea to keep the right wing strong. It is told in almost every history of the campaign and nobody can trace it to a reliable witness, so treat it as legend. But it survives because it captures exactly what his successor would fail to do.
That is the characteristic failure. Not the bold plan, and not the cautious plan, but the bold plan modified just enough by political anxiety to lose its own logic while keeping all of its risk.
ch.cap: Schlieffen's right wing swings through Belgium on paper

b: France had the mirror-image disease. After the humiliation of 1870 the French army had spent forty years concluding that it had lost through passivity, and a generation of officers around Colonel de Grandmaison built a doctrine out of that conclusion: attaque à outrance, attack to the uttermost. Will, dash, élan. Plan XVII, adopted in 1913, was an immediate general offensive into Alsace-Lorraine, and the doctrine ran so deep that the army deliberately under-invested in heavy artillery, because heavy guns were defensive and therefore un-French.

The detail Tuchman uses to make it unforgettable is the uniform. Before 1914 the army debated replacing the dark blue coat and bright madder-red trousers that made an infantryman visible at a thousand yards, while the Germans had gone to field grey and the British to khaki. A former war minister appeared before a parliamentary commission and declared that the red trouser was France. The trousers stayed.

In the Battle of the Frontiers in the second half of August 1914, French infantry advanced in those colours into entrenched machine guns and quick-firing artillery, and France lost in the order of three hundred thousand men in about a fortnight, among the bloodiest weeks any army has ever had.
A doctrine had become an identity, and once that happens the evidence against it reads as an attack on who you are.
ch.cap: French infantry in red trousers charge into machine guns

ch.h: Your Majesty, it cannot be done
b: Mobilisation in 1914 meant moving millions of men and animals by rail on schedules worked out years in advance to the quarter-hour. Eleven thousand trains in the German case. The plans were so intricate that they could neither be partially executed nor improvised.

On the afternoon of 1 August, Kaiser Wilhelm II was handed a telegram which seemed to suggest Britain might keep France out of the war, and stay out itself, if Germany attacked only Russia. Delighted, he called for champagne and told Moltke to turn the army east.

Moltke refused. The deployment could not be redirected, he said; the whole army would become a disorganised mass of armed men with no supplies. He later wrote that he felt as if his heart were breaking. The Kaiser snapped at him that his uncle would have given a different answer.

The telegram turned out to rest on a misunderstanding in any case. But hold the scene, because it is the most instructive thirty seconds in the book. The most powerful man in Europe wanted to stop. His chief of staff wanted to obey. And the answer was that it was no longer possible, because the point of no return had been passed days earlier by a decision nobody experienced as final at the time.
ch.cap: Moltke refuses: the trains cannot be turned east

b: On 2 August Germany handed Belgium an ultimatum demanding free passage, with a twelve-hour deadline. The calculation was straightforward: Belgium had six divisions against the largest army in Europe, would protest for the record, and would stand aside.

King Albert and his government refused. The invasion began on 4 August. The ring of forts at Liège, which the Germans expected to reduce in two days, held for over a week against siege howitzers of a calibre nobody had seen before, and while the military delay was smaller than legend has it, the political consequence was enormous. Germany had violated the neutrality Britain guaranteed by treaty in 1839, which the German chancellor dismissed as a scrap of paper, and which brought in Britain, the Empire, and the Royal Navy's blockade.

The smallest actor in the calculation produced the largest deviation from the plan, and it did so not through force but through refusal. Nothing in the German staff work had a column for a small country declining on principle to be walked over.

Britain's own decision came on the evening of 3 August. The Foreign Secretary, Sir Edward Grey, is said to have stood at a window in Whitehall watching the street lamps being lit and remarked that the lamps were going out all over Europe. The line comes from his own memoirs, written a decade later, and may have been polished in the remembering. The next day Britain sent Germany an ultimatum of its own, and at eleven that night, London time, it expired. Lord Kitchener, the new Secretary of State for War, startled his colleagues by predicting a war of at least three years that would need armies of millions. Almost everyone else expected it to be over within months.

Keep that as a general warning about plans built on other people's expected rationality. The weakest party in any arrangement is the one whose behaviour you have modelled least carefully, and refusal is always available to them.
ch.cap: Liège's forts hold under fire, the Belgian flag flying

ch.h: The two corps that went east
b: Then the Russians came early. The German plan assumed Russia would need six weeks or more to mobilise. Instead two Russian armies invaded East Prussia in the middle of August, before they were properly ready, because France had begged its ally to attack as fast as possible. Refugees streamed west and panic reached Berlin.

On 25 August, with his right wing in France already short of the strength Schlieffen had demanded, Moltke ordered two army corps taken out of it and sent east by train. They arrived too late to matter. By then the Germans in East Prussia, under Hindenburg and Ludendorff, had surrounded and destroyed General Samsonov's army at Tannenberg, helped by Russian radio orders sent uncoded and read by German listeners. Samsonov walked into the forest and shot himself.

In the west the right wing, thinned by the very commander charged with protecting it, swung inside Paris rather than round it. Joffre, the stolid French commander who had kept his nerve and his regular meals through a fortnight of disaster, saw the exposed flank and counter-attacked on the Marne from 6 September, alongside the British and with troops rushed out from Paris, some of them, famously, in requisitioned taxis. The taxis carried only a few thousand men and their military value was small. Their value as a story was enormous.

Within days the German armies were falling back to the Aisne, and Moltke, exhausted and by several accounts close to collapse, was quietly replaced by Erich von Falkenhayn. The men dug in. Tuchman ends her book here, at the trenches, and her verdict is that the Marne decided not who would win but that the war would go on, for four more years.
ch.cap: Paris taxis race to the Marne as trains rush east

ch.h: Kennedy's copy, and where she is wrong
b: In 1962 John F. Kennedy read the book and could not stop talking about it. He bought copies for his cabinet and senior officers and asked them to read it. According to Robert McNamara, what struck the president was that the men of 1914 had not chosen their war, they had bungled into one none of them wanted. Weeks later came the Cuban missile crisis, during which Kennedy repeatedly sought ways to give Khrushchev room to retreat rather than forcing a binary choice. Nobody can prove a book prevented a nuclear exchange. It remains the strongest available case for reading history as a practical discipline.

Now the objections, because they are serious. The first is determinism: reviewers from the 1960s onwards objected that she draws long, tidy causal chains across decades, most notoriously from the escape of the Goeben to the later history of the Middle East, in a way that makes outcomes look more inevitable than the evidence supports. The second is sourcing: she leaned heavily on memoirs, which are precisely the documents in which generals explain why the disaster was not their fault, and made less use of staff archives. The third is omission: the Balkans and the Austro-Russian quarrel that actually started the war get little space.

And the fourth is the big one. Margaret MacMillan, writing in the centenary years, praised the narrative and then noted that Tuchman's central explanation, entangling alliances plus rigid timetables equals inevitable war, is no longer what most historians think. Christopher Clark's The Sleepwalkers restores agency: decisions were taken, by identifiable men, who had alternatives.
Which leaves you with the pattern you met yesterday. Take the mechanism, plans that cannot be stopped, doctrine hardened into identity, the unmodelled small actor, and check the causes yourself.
ch.cap: Kennedy reads Tuchman weeks before the Cuban missile crisis

take: Catastrophes are run by competent people

Nine reigning kings rode through London in 1910; four years later three of their empires were gone. Stop hunting for the villain or the idiot in a failure and look at the design that made capable people behave that way.
Beware the plan with no smaller version

The Schlieffen Plan only worked at full speed, in one direction, all at once. Write down the smallest viable version of each of your current commitments; where none exists, change the structure rather than raising your confidence.
A hedged bold plan is the worst of both

Moltke strengthened the left wing for political reasons and weakened the one thing the plan depended on, keeping all the risk and losing the logic. Either commit to the design or replace it, do not soften it until it cannot work.

Le pantalon rouge, c'est la France, and three hundred thousand men were lost in a fortnight advancing in colours visible at a thousand yards. When a practice becomes who you are, evidence against it is received as an insult, so watch for the belief you would feel personally attacked to lose.

On 1 August the Kaiser wanted to stop and could not, because eleven thousand trains were already moving. For every committing operation, write down now the point of no return and the metric you will check the day before it, and diarise that date.
Your weakest counterparty can wreck the plan

Belgium had six divisions and brought in the British Empire by refusing. The party whose behaviour you have modelled least carefully is your largest source of variance, and refusal is always available to them.

Tuchman's claim is that thirty days of indecisive fighting produced the deadlock, the casualty arithmetic, Versailles and the 1930s. Early configuration is disproportionately durable, an argument for going slowly at the start of anything and revisiting founding decisions you have stopped noticing.
History is a practical discipline or nothing
Kennedy handed the book to his cabinet and then spent the missile crisis looking for ways to let the other side retreat. Read for the mechanism you can use on Monday, not for the anecdote.
recall: Why does Tuchman open with the funeral of Edward VII?

Because the nine reigning kings riding behind the coffin were cousins, professionals and in no way mad, and four years later three of those empires had ceased to exist. Opening there denies the reader a villain and forces attention onto the design rather than the people.
What single property made the Schlieffen Plan so dangerous, and what did Moltke do to it?

It only functioned at full speed, in one direction, executed completely, there was no partial version. Moltke kept it but strengthened the left wing in Alsace-Lorraine for political reasons, weakening the right wing the whole concept depended on, so it retained its risk and lost its logic.
Describe the exchange of 1 August 1914 and state its significance.

The Kaiser, believing Britain might stay out if Germany attacked only Russia, ordered Moltke to turn the army east. Moltke refused: the deployment of millions could not be improvised. The significance is that the point of no return had been crossed days earlier by decisions nobody experienced as final, so the most powerful man in Europe wanted to stop and could not.
Why did Moltke send two corps east in August 1914, and what did it cost?

Two Russian armies invaded East Prussia far sooner than the German plan assumed, and on 25 August Moltke took two corps from his right wing to meet them. They arrived after Tannenberg had already been won, and their absence weakened the very wing that then failed on the Marne.
What is Tuchman's verdict on the Battle of the Marne?

She ends the book with it and argues that it decided not who would win the war but that the war would continue. The Germans fell back, Moltke was replaced, both sides dug in, and four more years of trench warfare followed.
note: Documented: her birth in 1912, the family connection to Ambassador Henry Morgenthau, the steamer's arrival at Constantinople on 10 August 1914 and her presence aboard (which she confirmed in Practicing History), Radcliffe 1933, the two Pulitzers, her death in 1989. Kennedy's distribution of the book rests chiefly on McNamara's recollection. The Moltke quotation is given as Tuchman renders the exchange, not as a verbatim transcript, and Grey's lamps remark comes from his own memoirs of 1925, so may have been polished. The taxis of the Marne carried only a few thousand men. Principal counter-arguments: Oron Hale on determinism, Margaret MacMillan, and Christopher Clark's The Sleepwalkers.
words: Energetic style, dash and confident enthusiasm.
French doctrine before 1914 held that élan and the will to attack would beat machine guns, and the Battle of the Frontiers proved it wrong.
A military manoeuvre that swings round an enemy's flank to attack from the side or rear and trap them.
The Schlieffen Plan was a vast envelopment, a right wing wheeling through Belgium to come round behind Paris.
An act or event used to justify going to war.
Germany's violation of Belgian neutrality, guaranteed by treaty in 1839, gave Britain its casus belli.
The view that events are fixed by prior causes, so that what happened was bound to happen.
Critics charge Tuchman with determinism for drawing tidy chains from 1914 decisions to outcomes decades later.
Pushing a dangerous confrontation to the edge of disaster to force the other side to back down.
Kennedy read the book as a warning against brinkmanship with no exit, and in the Cuban missile crisis kept looking for ways to let Khrushchev retreat.

biz: Fit the brake before the trains move

Moltke could not stop because the point of no return had been passed days earlier, without anyone feeling it. In debt advice the equivalent is a solution that is hard to undo, such as an IVA, which binds a client for years once creditors approve it. Before any case goes to Assist My Finances, add a short check, ideally on a separate call: has the client heard the alternatives, such as a debt management plan, a debt relief order, bankruptcy or Breathing Space, in plain words? Has any vulnerability been recorded and acted on? Track how many clients change course at that check, and why.
When a habit becomes who you are

The French kept their red trousers because changing them felt like betraying France. Every firm has its version: a script, a channel or a way of working that has become part of its identity. Perhaps it is phoning every HomeownersLoan enquiry straight away, when some homeowners would rather message on WhatsApp at ten at night. Test it: from this week, ask each new enquiry how they prefer to be contacted, honour the answer, and after a month compare contact rates and completed applications by preference. If the result irritates you, that is the sign it had become doctrine.
connects: Perrow's tightly coupled systems, where one step forces the next with no time to intervene, describe the mobilisation timetables of 1914 that could not be paused once started.
Clausewitz's friction, the gap between the plan on paper and war in practice, is what undid the Schlieffen Plan when Belgium resisted and Russia arrived early.
Tetlock's finding that confident experts often forecast badly fits the consensus of 1914 that the war would be short, which Kitchener almost alone rejected.
recap:
On the tenth of August, nineteen fourteen, a little Italian steamer arrived in Constantinople carrying a two-year-old girl called Barbara Wertheim, granddaughter of the American ambassador. On its way it had sailed into the middle of a naval chase that helped drag Turkey into the First World War. Nearly fifty years later that girl, now Barbara Tuchman, wrote the most famous book about the war's first month, and never mentioned that she had been there.

She was an amateur in the proper sense. She took a degree at Radcliffe, never did a doctorate, worked as a journalist, raised three daughters, and only turned to history properly in her forties. The Guns of August appeared in nineteen sixty-two, when she was fifty, and won a Pulitzer Prize. That same year President Kennedy read it, handed copies to his officials, and weeks later, in the Cuban missile crisis, kept looking for ways to let the Soviet leader back down.

The book opens with nine kings riding behind a royal coffin in London in nineteen ten. Cousins, most of them, educated, none of them mad. That is the first idea. Catastrophes are usually made by competent people inside a bad design, so look for the mechanism, not the villain.

The second is the plan with no smaller version. Germany's Schlieffen Plan only worked at full speed, through Belgium, all at once. Its keeper, Moltke, then weakened it for political comfort, keeping all of the risk and losing the logic.

The third is doctrine hardening into identity. The French believed in attack at all costs, and sent infantry in bright red trousers into machine guns. Around three hundred thousand men were lost in about a fortnight.

The fourth is the missing brake. On the first of August the Kaiser wanted to stop, and his chief of staff told him eleven thousand trains could not be turned round. The point of no return had been passed days earlier, and nobody had noticed.

And the fifth is the small player nobody modelled. Belgium was expected to protest and step aside. It refused, and its refusal brought the British Empire into the war.

Historians now argue that Tuchman made the war look more inevitable than it was, and that real men made real choices with real alternatives. Keep that in mind. But keep the mechanism too.

The line to remember is this. The time to fit the brake is before the trains start moving.
